World.title: Pemex net profit plunges 70% in Q2 despite debt reduction
World.content:
Pemex’s net profit declined almost 70% annually in the second quarter of 2026, but the heavily indebted state oil company nevertheless asserted that it recorded “favorable results” in the period.

In a filing with the Mexican Stock Exchange on Friday, Pemex reported a net profit of 18.02 billion pesos (US $1.04 billion) between April and June, a decline of 69.7% compared to the second quarter of 2025.

📰 Comunicado Nacional | PEMEX registra resultados operativos y financieros favorables durante el segundo trimestre de 2026

🔗 https://t.co/aPIRDBLOM0 pic.twitter.com/pspHmI5YeQ — Petróleos Mexicanos (@Pemex) July 31, 2026

Pemex said that the lower profit was due to a 177% annual increase in its financial costs, higher tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate, with the peso strengthening around 2.5% against the US dollar in the second quarter of the year.

Despite the near 70% decline in its net profit, Pemex said in a statement on Friday that it recorded “favorable results in its main operational and financial indicators” in the second quarter.

“In an international environment of high volatility, the company maintained its production base, recorded higher levels of industrial transformation [i.e. refining] and guaranteed supply to the national market,” Pemex said.

The state oil company said that between April and June:

Its “total production of hydrocarbons averaged 2.477 million barrels of crude oil equivalent per day,” an annual increase of 4.6%.

Its production of liquid hydrocarbons averaged 1.658 million barrels per day (bpd), “supported by strategic fields such as Ixachi, Bakté, Itta, Koban and Maloob.” (This level of production is short of the government’s 1.8 million bpd goal and represents a decline compared to 2025.)

Its processing of crude at refineries increased 2.9% annually to 1.008 million bpd.

Its national sales of oil and oil products increased 9.8% annually to 1.471 million bpd.

Its income from sales and services rose 30.3% annually to 510.4 billion pesos (US $29.45 billion).

Its operating profit was 85.5 billion pesos (US $4.93 billion), a significant improvement from a 11 billion-peso loss in the second quarter of 2025.

Pemex also reported that its debt at June 30 was US $77.5 billion, a reduction of 9.1% compared to the end of 2025.

“In addition, short-term debt accounted for a smaller share of total debt, easing immediate financial pressures and strengthening the company’s financial flexibility. This is consistent with Pemex’s commitment to maintaining zero net debt,” the state oil company said.

Pemex is aiming to increase oil production, including via partnerships with private companies, as the federal government seeks to reach self-sufficiency for fuel. However, Reuters reported on Friday that “progress has been slower than hoped and uncertainty remains over how quickly new projects can contribute meaningful volumes.”

The news agency also said that Pemex “has increasingly directed production to domestic refineries as part ⁠of the ​government’s push for energy self-sufficiency, even as stronger ​oil prices could make exports more lucrative.”

In addition, Reuters reported that “Pemex is struggling to reverse years of declining output while it tries ​to reduce its financial obligations to bondholders, banks, suppliers and contractors.”

Citing the company’s Mexican Stock Exchange filing, Reuters said that as of June 30, Pemex ‌”had ⁠restructured 255.39 billion pesos [US $14.74 billion] of supplier debt incurred in 2025 under an eight-year payment scheme.”

The federal government has provided ample financial support for Pemex in recent years, and President Claudia Sheinbaum asserted in February that the company had “recovered” after former Mexican governments “dedicated 36 years to trying to disappear” it between 1982 and 2018.

When announcing a cut to Mexico’s sovereign credit rating in May, Moody’s warned that “continued support for Pemex will continue to limit fiscal consolidation.”

One new partnership that the federal government hopes will lead to a boost in oil production is that between Pemex and Brazil’s Petrobras, which are set to collaborate on deep-water exploration and extraction in the Gulf of Mexico.

With reports from AFP, El Economista and Reuters

World.title: Why is Chihuahua working on water projects with Israel?
World.content:
A water cooperation agreement between the Chihuahua state government and the Israeli international cooperation agency MASHAV has become the center of social conflict and the cause of growing protests amid extreme water stress in the state.

On Saturday, protesters called by the Save the Hills of Chihuahua and the Feminist Assembly marched through the streets of the capital city of Chihuahua, accusing the state government and the Central Water and Sanitation Board (JCAS) of promoting Zionism and doing business with a government they accuse of committing genocide in Gaza.

The demonstrations were part of a nationwide day of action involving at least 14 states, where protesters called for a ceasefire in Gaza and demanded that the Mexican government end diplomatic and trade relations with Israel.

At the center of the controversy is a signed cooperation agreement dated February 2023 between the JCAS of Chihuahua and MASHAV, part of the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Valid until 2027, the agreement establishes the exchange of knowledge and technology for the design, construction and maintenance of water systems in crisis conditions, as well as improvements in the reuse of treated water, efficiency in drinking water, sanitation and sustainable agriculture.

The agreement allows participation of the Israeli private sector in water-related projects in Chihuahua. Although the agreement is presented as a technical cooperation plan, activists claim that it facilitates contracts and business opportunities for Israeli companies in the state’s water infrastructure.

Opponents also argue that the Chihuahua government did not register the international agreement with the Ministry of Foreign Relations (SRE), which would make it illegal in Mexico.

However, Governor Maru Campos Galván and head of JCAS Mario Mata Carrasco stated that the agreement is not a legally binding document and does not create any legally binding obligations or benefits for the parties involved.

Rather, they say it is a technical cooperation mechanism for sharing knowledge without granting rights, concessions or control over the state’s water — meaning there wouldn’t be an obligation to register the agreement with the SRE.

According to Mexican law, non-binding international agreements are not necessarily subject to the same registration requirements as treaties or other legally binding agreements. Nonetheless, the SRE suggests a similar registration procedure to ensure consistency with Mexico’s foreign policy, meaning such agreements wouldn’t necessarily appear in the SRE’s treaty database.

For the state government, this international agreement means an opportunity to learn from Israel’s experience in water treatment, reuse and desalination processes to strengthen the hydraulic infrastructure of Chihuahua, especially given the drought conditions the state is currently facing.

With reports from La Jornada, Expansión, Enfoque Noticias and SPD Noticias

World.title: The Batopilas story: 50 years in a Mexican silver mine
World.content:
In 1938, Grant Shepherd, son of Alexander Robey Shepherd, “The father of modern Washington, D.C.,” published his memoirs. The book “The Silver Magnet — 50 Years in a Mexican Silver Mine” (E.P. Dutton and Co., 1938) gives us a first-hand look at life in a fabulously rich mine located next to an impossibly remote town around the start of the Mexican Revolution.

Fortunately, the historical value of Shepherd’s book was noted by the American Council of Learned Societies and digitally reformatted for the Humanities E-Book project, making it available from many libraries. This, however, does not mean “The Silver Magnet” is a scholarly work. Not at all. What we have here are rambling memoirs: the recollections of a man who, over a period of 60 years, lived life to its fullest in a remote corner of Mexico that — even today — is difficult to reach.

Anyone interested in Mexico and silver mines will find many a rich nugget here. Let’s take a peek at a few of them.

How to carry a piano down a canyon wall

In Shepherd’s day, to reach Batopilas, Chihuahua from the U.S., you had to ride 241 kilometers in wagons or oxcarts and then brace yourself for a further 300 kilometers on the backs of mules, ending in a narrow switchback trail down the labyrinthine gorges of the Copper Canyon, an elevation difference of 1,708 meters — greater than the average depth of the Grand Canyon.

So when the family decided to buy an upright piano, they faced the problem of how to transport it in one piece to Batopilas, a name that in Rarámuri means “river in a box.”

“All you need to solve a problem like this,” says Shepherd, is “a clever Mexican and an Indian … and if you leave it to them with no suggestions on your part, that cumbersome box will eventually arrive, and arrive right side up.”

Here’s the solution: Cut two long, straight pine poles. Put one on either side of the piano in its wooden box and tie them in such a way that the weight is balanced with no tendency to be top-heavy. Now put two men at each corner of the box.

“They get under the poles in a squatting position. At the word ‘Vámonos!’ they straighten up. The piano is off the ground, and the carriers move off with inward satisfaction of knowing that all they have to do now is to carry this great box for 185 miles in 15 or 20 days.”

For this, Shepherd adds, the men were paid US $1 a day plus first-class meals, which they considered fabulous pay for such an easy job.

How to filch silver from a mine

The ore at the Batopilas mines was very high grade, so there was always a chance that a miner would try to take a little of it home.

“Say, for instance, you wear your hair quite long … and you clean your hands to rid them of the mud caused by the cutting of the drill bit moistened by the water you squirt from your mouth into the hole; if you succeed in cleaning your hands by wiping them on your head, the long hair will get full of mud. When you go home and wash your hair in a basin, you will find that there remain in the basin fine particles of silver. After you become expert at it, you will be able to run it up to as much as 50 cents worth a day. If you are diligent, this will increase your weekly income by about US $3.”

Note that an unskilled laborer was paid a minimum wage of US $1.50 per day.

How not to turn on a lightbulb

Unbelievable as it may sound, in 1889, little Batopilas, population 6,500, was the second city in Mexico to get electric lights (after the capital), thanks to the Americans running the mines.

Shepherd recalls: “One of the men was told to go out and touch a button to light up the place that first night the electric light plant was put into commission. He got a box of matches and tried to screw off the glass bulb so he could apply a match to the wire — and put the bulb into the vise to hold it. There was a pop and a crack. He sprang back from this mysterious thing, fell over a wheelbarrow that was directly behind him, and broke his arm! For a long time afterwards, he was known as Luz Eléctrica, Electric light.”

How to remain invisible while bathing

Shepherd also describes customs of the day unrelated to mining:

“The extreme modesty of the Mexican women was never more apparent than when they were bathing in the river. They carry an ordinary sheet, squat down with the middle of the sheet on top of their heads, spread it out over them, remove all of their clothing, put on an ankle-length cotton slip. (All of this is done underneath the tent made from the sheet.) Then, walking down into the river in this squatting position … they perform their ablutions. No one ever saw so much as the point of one of their toes!”

Cardsharps and Pancho Villa

“The Silver Magnet” touches on many other subjects: buried treasure, dynamite, cockfighting, cardsharps, the vileness of Pancho Villa and the excellence of Porfirio Díaz, plus everything you ever wanted to know about saddles, stirrups and chaps … but not a word about silicosis, which killed the majority of full-time miners before middle age.

The book ends with the death of Shepherd’s father, whose body was hand-carried 300 kilometers up the winding trail by local people who volunteered to do this without pay.

“The Silver Magnet” was reprinted many times. With luck, you may find a physical copy on a dusty shelf of your local bookstore.

World.title: Insecurity and bad weather battered Sinaloa’s economy in Q1 2026
World.content:
Insecurity and adverse weather conditions have wrought havoc on the economy of Sinaloa, a state where rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel have been engaged in a bloody battle since 2024.

The economy of the northern state contracted 4.5% on a quarter-over-quarter basis in the first three months of 2026, the national statistics agency INEGI reported last week.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, 20 recorded sequential contractions in the first quarter of the year, but Sinaloa’s economic result was easily the worst. On an annual basis, the northern state’s economy contracted 1.2% in the first three months of 2026, Sinaloa’s worst first quarter result since 2021.

Adriana García, economic analysis coordinator at the Mexico City-based think tank México ¿cómo vamos?, told the newspaper El Universal that the poor economic results in Sinaloa are mainly due to insecurity. Violence has dampened investment in the state and stifled the opening of new businesses, she said.

“Insecurity hinders economic activity,” García told El Universal.

Cristina Ibarra, president of the Mexican Federation of Collegiate Economists, also said that Sinaloa’s poor economic performance is linked to insecurity.

“The economic recovery strategy in Sinaloa simply hasn’t worked. Companies look for the best way to remain open, but there are a lot of disruptions caused by insecurity,” Ibarra told Espejo, a magazine based in state capital Culiacán, a city considered unsafe by more than 90% of residents, according to a recent INEGI survey.

The main cause of insecurity in Sinaloa is the ongoing feud between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos, rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel, the largest and most powerful drug trafficking organization in the Western Hemisphere, according to Insight Crime.

A long-running battle between the two factions intensified in 2024 after Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López, forced onto a private plane and flown to the United States, where both Zambada and Guzmán were arrested.

Zambada was the leader of Los Mayos, while Guzmán López, a son of convicted drug lord and Sinaloa Cartel founder Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera, was a leader of Los Chapitos along with three of his brothers.

The “war” between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos has claimed well over 2,000 lives and caused the disappearance of thousands more people since September 2024.

In addition to causing the Sinaloa economy to tank in the first quarter of this year, data shows that the cartel-related violence has affected employment in the northern state. Sinaloa shed almost 27,000 formal sector positions in the first half of 2026, the biggest loss of jobs among the 32 federal entities. As a result, the state’s informal economy has been growing rapidly.

“Establishments are closing or reducing their operational personnel due to insecurity,” García told El Universal.

“… Better security results are needed so that sinaloenses can return to their normal activities,” she said.

In the first six months of 2026, Sinaloa ranked as the fourth most violent state in Mexico in terms of total homicides, with 633, even as murders declined 28.3% annually in the state.

In early May, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya decided to go on leave after he and various other officials were formally accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors. Three months later, Rocha hasn’t returned to the job.

Sinaloa primary sector contracts 16.6% annually

INEGI’s data shows that the primary sector in Sinaloa contracted 16.6% in annual terms in the first quarter of 2026. The secondary sector grew 5.2% while the tertiary sector expanded 0.8%.

“There was a lot less production in the state due to weather-related issues [including drought],” Jesús Rojo, president of the Sinaloa Confederation of Agricultural Associations, told the Espejo magazine.

“Not just in corn,” Rojo said. “In the mango sector, the orchards didn’t bloom sufficiently.”

While drought conditions have recently eased in Sinaloa, around one-quarter of the state’s territory remains abnormally dry, according to the National Water Commission.

Jesús Márquez Rojas, a research economist and assistant vice president with Banamex, told El Universal that beef production in Sinaloa is also down. In addition, high prices for tomatoes in early 2026 had an adverse impact on producers in Sinaloa, he said.

A decline in agricultural production levels in Sinaloa — nicknamed el granero de México, or Mexico’s breadbasket — affects other parts of the state’s economy, including the transport and packing industries.

How are other state economies performing?

Only 12 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities grew in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the final three-month period of 2025.

They were:

Colima: +3%

Michoacán: +1.7%

Baja California Sur: +1.6%

Durango: +1.2%

Tlaxcala: +1%

Guanajuato: +0.9% (Guanajuato is Mexico’s most violent state in terms of total homicides)

Chiapas: +0.7%

México state: +0.7%

Hidalgo: +0.5%

Puebla: +0.5%

Yucatán: +0.4%

Tamaulipas: +0.3%

The 20 entities that recorded quarter-over-quarter contractions in the first three months of 2026 were:

Sinaloa: -4.5%

Oaxaca: -3.1%

Mexico City: -2.9%

Zacatecas: -2.4%

Tabasco: -2.1%

Nayarit: -2%

Quintana Roo: -1.9%

Chihuahua: -1.8%

San Luis Potosí: -1.4%

Nuevo León: -1.3%

Coahuila: -1.2%

Jalisco: -0.8%

Morelos: -0.8%

Veracruz: -0.7%

Guerrero: -0.7%

Querétaro: -0.6%

Campeche: -0.6%

Baja California: -0.5%

Aguascalientes: -0.2%

Sonora: -0.1%

The Mexican economy as a whole contracted 0.6% in the first quarter of the year compared to the October-December period of 2025. The economy grew 1.5% sequentially in the second quarter and 2.1% on an annual basis.

On an annual basis, Hidalgo was Mexico’s fastest-growing state in the first quarter of 2026, its economy expanding 7.4% in the period. Tamaulipas ranked second (+5.4%), followed by Colima (+4%), Tabasco (+3.3%) and Puebla (+2.7%).

The state that recorded the worst economic result in annual terms in the first quarter was Campeche, where GDP fell 5.2%. The next worst results were in Coahuila (-4.7%), Morelos (-3.1%), Quintana Roo (-2.9%) and Oaxaca (-2.8%).

With reports from El Universal and Revista Espejo

World.title: Tulum, known for its beaches and Maya ruins, is named the happiest travel destination in the world
World.content:
A detailed analysis of more than a million travel reviews has led an Irish travel insurance company to conclude that Tulum — one of the more laid-back beach resorts on Mexico’s Caribbean coast — is the happiest travel destination on earth.

The company, JustCover, pored through written comments on all kinds of tourist attractions — national parks, entertainment venues, scenic places and urban areas, as well as resorts — looking for vocabulary such as “happy” and “joy.”

Based on their research, they assigned a “Happy Place Score” to each destination on a scale of 0 to 100. Tulum ended up with a perfect 100 out of 100 score.

Tulum has indeed become extremely popular in recent years as a more tranquil option to bustling Cancún in Quintana Roo state. JustCover mentioned Tulum’s preserved Maya ruins, perched on a cliff overlooking the Caribbean Sea, its nature reserves and picturesque view.

“Tulum also draws visitors with its thriving food, nightlife and wellness scene,” the company pointed out.

Tulum boasts several smaller resorts and boutique hotels, which many tourists are opting for over Cancún’s giant all-inclusive resorts and beach clubs. It also offers a wide range of adventure and eco-tourism attractions, including cenotes and a lazy river.

Travel + Leisure’s World’s Best Awards 2025 list of the best resorts in Mexico featured both the Conrad Tulum Riviera Maya and La Zebra Tulum.

The town is also home to some of Mexico’s most well-regarded restaurants, with several spots mentioned in the Michelin Guide.

While Tulum came out on top in terms of happiness, Oaxaca was also given a high score for its “food, markets, and its deep Indigenous culture,” ranking in third place.

JustCover’s top 10 Happy Place Destinations are as follows:

Tulum, Mexico Soufrière, Saint Lucia Oaxaca, Mexico Las Vegas Maui, Hawaii New York City Cappadocia, Turkey Rio de Janeiro Chicago Toronto

With reports from Travel + Leisure and USA Today

World.title: Riot breaks out at Tapachula migrant detention center after alleged arson attempt
World.content:
Two migrants were arrested on charges of inciting a riot at an immigration holding center in the southern state of Chiapas on Saturday night. The two men were arrested and transferred to Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the state capital, where they were being processed for immediate deportation.

The incident occurred at the Siglo XXI Migration Station in the border town of Tapachula — the largest immigration detention center in Latin America — where approximately 40 migrants were being processed after being detained in different parts of the country.

The National Migration Institute (INM) said the two men in question — reportedly Venezuelan nationals — began displaying aggressive behavior, prompting a broader disturbance in the station.

The newly arrived migrants began demanding their immediate release, later claiming to be victims of systematic abuse and incommunicado detention.

While agents attempted to calm the tumult, the men are alleged to have attempted to set a mattress on fire.

INM agents, state and municipal security forces and emergency services required more than two hours to quell the uprising, but officials reported that no detainees were injured.

Luis García Villagrán, a human rights activist with the Center for Human Dignity AC, expressed skepticism about the incident, saying the INM often holds migrants incommunicado for periods of up to 10 days and denies them access to legal defense.

“There is a terrible lack of transparency about what is happening at this Immigration Station,” he told the newspaper La Jornada.

The organization said that some 65,000 migrants — many of whom are deported from the U.S. and transferred by land to Tapachula or the INM station in Villahermosa, Tabasco — are stranded in southern Mexico awaiting resolution of their cases. They are processed at these facilities and eventually released, but not permitted to travel outside the area.

The disturbance inside the facility reignited complaints about overcrowding, lack of due process and alleged human rights violations at Siglo XXI which is designed to hold up to 1,500 people.

There have been at least five previous incidents of riots and protests at Siglo XXI, including in April 2019, when migrants rioted, took control of the facilities, and nearly 1,300 migrants escaped.

The attempt to set fire to mattresses was particularly disturbing as it brought to mind the March 23, 2023, fire at a migrant facility in Cd. Juárez that resulted in the death of 40 migrants.

With reports from El Financiero, La Jornada, Proceso, El Economista and El Heraldo de México

World.title: Sheinbaum invites author of ‘The Anxious Generation’ to explain social media’s impacts on kids: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📺 Canal Once occupation ends: Education Minister Mario Delgado said that Canal Once workers peacefully retook the station’s facilities on Sunday, more than two months after IPN students began occupying them, forcing out six protesters; he said the station’s audiovisual archive appears damaged, with material “broken and disorganized on the floor.”

Education Minister Mario Delgado said that Canal Once workers peacefully retook the station’s facilities on Sunday, more than two months after IPN students began occupying them, forcing out six protesters; he said the station’s audiovisual archive appears damaged, with material “broken and disorganized on the floor.” 💰 Sheinbaum alleges paid protest: The president asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once, saying investigations have not yet determined who made the payments, and called it illogical for a student movement focused on IPN improvements to seize the TV station for so long.

The president asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once, saying investigations have not yet determined who made the payments, and called it illogical for a student movement focused on IPN improvements to seize the TV station for so long. 📱 Social media debate explained: Sheinbaum said the government opened a public debate on children’s use of social media because studies show excessive use — particularly infinite scrolling and short videos — creates addiction, though she stressed technology also has “extraordinary uses” like global communication and virtual museum visits.

Sheinbaum said the government opened a public debate on children’s use of social media because studies show excessive use — particularly infinite scrolling and short videos — creates addiction, though she stressed technology also has “extraordinary uses” like global communication and virtual museum visits. 🧠 Haidt warns of “digital pacifier”: U.S. psychologist Jonathan Haidt addressed the mañanera, calling children’s social media and touchscreen use a “public health problem” and urging parents not to give kids access to phones until at least age four to six, citing damage to cognitive development.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Monday morning press conference came two weeks after the federal government announced three regional forums to canvass views on children’s use of social media and artificial intelligence tools and platforms ahead of drafting a legislative proposal to regulate these technologies.

At today’s mañanera, Sheinbaum explained why the government initiated a public debate on young people’s use of social media. Two weeks ago, she said that a consultation process with experts, parents, teachers, young people and others should lead to “some scheme of regulation” on the use of social media by minors.

It is not yet known whether the government will seek to ban young people under a certain age from using social media as part of a legislative proposal that could be submitted to Congress later this year. However, Education Minister Mario Delgado, who was at today’s mañanera, said earlier this year that the Mexican government was exploring the possibility of imposing age restrictions.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were the remarks made by both Sheinbaum and Delgado about a lengthy student takeover of the public television station Canal Once.

Student takeover of Canal Once ends

A reporter noted that workers with Canal Once, a public television network owned by the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), returned to their workplace on Sunday more than two months after a group of IPN students began occupying the TV station’s facilities as part of a protest against alleged financial mismanagement at the university, among other alleged problems.

Protesting students allege that they were violently forced out of Canal Once’s Mexico City facilities on Sunday.

Asked her opinion about the situation, Sheinbaum referred the question to her education minister.

Delgado said that “a group of young people” from IPN decided to occupy the Canal Once facilities on May 20.

“We made many attempts to establish dialogue with them,” he said before highlighting that discussions took place and asserting that none of the students’ demands were related to Canal Once.

Consequently, Delgado said that authorities asked the protesting students to leave Canal Once — which has an extensive audiovisual archive — but they repeatedly refused to do so.

He said that Canal Once workers on Sunday “decided to organize themselves” to “peacefully” retake the television station’s facilities. They achieved their goal, forcing six remaining student protesters out of Canal Once.

“Unfortunately, at first glance, there is damage to the archive,” Delgado said.

“There is material broken and disorganized on the floor,” he said.

“But we’re going to wait to see how serious this damage is. And we said to the young people that we’re going to continue with the roundtable discussions, but it’s not possible for a TV station that belongs to the people of Mexico to remain seized,” Delgado said.

He didn’t say whether the protesting students would face criminal charges for occupying Canal Once and allegedly damaging its archive.

Sheinbaum asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once.

“On one occasion we presented here about how these students received resources, money,” she said, adding that investigations had not yet determined who made the alleged payments.

“It’s not logical that a student movement that is asking for improvements in the Polytechnic [Institute] occupies Canal Once for so long,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Fortunately, Canal Once never stopped broadcasting,” she said, explaining that the Ministry of Public Education lent equipment and studios to the public television station.

Sheinbaum: Technology has ‘extraordinary uses’ but social media is problematic

After presentations from experts on the impact of screen time and social media on children and adolescents, a reporter asked Sheinbaum her opinion about technology that can assist young people’s learning.

“What we’re seeing here are different studies that show that the excessive use of social media, particularly use linked to infinite scrolling … or [watching] short videos, creates addiction,” the president said.

She went on to say that no one can deny that technology has “extraordinary uses,” citing the ability to communicate with people on the other side of the world and virtually visit “the world’s best museums” as examples.

“The issue is that certain mechanisms of [social media] platforms are creating learning problems, cognitive development problems and addiction,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Mexicans can’t say ‘it’s OK.’ It’s something that we have to review for our daughters and sons, our granddaughters and grandsons,” she said.

“… That’s why we opened the debate,” Sheinbaum said.

Her remarks came after U.S. psychologist Jonathan Haidt — author of the 2024 book “The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness” — addressed the mañanera.

Among his remarks, Haidt said that “now we know that it’s terrible to give a young child a touchscreen because they learn to get quick dopamine just by touching, touching, touching.”

“… That means that when they don’t have the phone, they now are very upset,” he said.

“… In the United States, 40% of two-year-olds have their own iPad or iPhone and this is a terrible thing which we now know is damaging their development when they arrive at school. What I’m recommending whenever I’m able to speak to governments around the world is treat this as a public health problem,” Haidt said.

“… This is a public health problem and it is important to educate new mothers, new parents, that they should not use a digital pacifier. They should not give … [their children] access to any phones until they’re at least four, five, six,” he said.

World.title: MND Local: A new art space opens in Guadalajara’s Historic Center, and the latest effort to conserve the Primavera Forest
World.content:
This week, we report on a new proposal to protect the city’s green lung, the Bosque La Primavera (Primavera Forest), from real estate development, and a summer book sale. But first, let’s take a look at an exciting new cultural space in Guadalajara’s Historic Center.

Motor is a new cultural space in Guadalajara’s Historic Center

On Juan Manuel Street in Guadalajara’s center and protected cultural heritage zone, a historical gem dating back to 1850 has recently been restored and reimagined as a new cultural space for artists.

The building has a long and winding history. It initially served as a residence, but was later repurposed as a printing facility, and then a mechanical workshop. Its latest reincarnation is the work of local artist Claudio Limón, whose interest in architecture was sparked by his brother and romantic partner, both of whom are professional architects.

“My brother is passionate about the history of architecture, and he told me a lot about the Historic Center, about what has been lost and the different architectural styles of Guadalajara. Then I married an architect, too, and many of my friends are architects,” Limón recently told Mural.

Motor’s role in historic preservation

Dubbed Motor, the space represents not only a new venue for today’s local artists to create work, but Limón’s desire to contribute to the city’s historic preservation. The building now hosts a production studio, artist workshops (mostly allocated to locals, with one space for international residencies) and a space for rotating exhibitions.

The restoration process of the property where Motor is now located took seven months. The old mechanical workshop was preserved virtually intact and became the conceptual core of the project. The venue’s new name refers not only to the building’s industrial past, but also to a creative energy Limón hopes to trigger within the community.

“I want anyone who comes to an exhibition here to also visit the record store next door, buy books or get to know the neighboring businesses,” Limón explained.

Ultimately, the artist hopes Motor will stand as a counterpoint to the prevailing tendency toward tearing down and building anew, sparking enthusiasm for historic preservation in Guadalajara, where for decades the city has witnessed significant loss of its historical and artistic heritage.

A new proposal is introduced to protect a threatened part of Primavera Forest

Like an incurable chain smoker, Guadalajara has been doing serious damage to its “lungs” in recent years — i.e., developing rather than conserving many of its important green spaces. Now, a local congresswoman representing the Green Party of Mexico (PVEM) seeks to shift the narrative.

Congresswoman Brenda Carrera García presented a proposal earlier this month to protect La Primavera Forest from additional real estate development. Her proposed legislation would block new residential construction on a 60-hectare plot for a project marketed as “Santa Anita Hill” in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga.

The developer has planned to build a new community right in the transition zone of the Primavera Forest, a biosphere reserve with UNESCO status and an area that’s increasingly viewed as critical to safeguarding the Guadalajara metropolitan area’s water supply. The land is home to 20,000 oak trees that are fundamental to recharging the area’s aquifers, absorbing seasonal rainfall and mitigating the city’s chronic air pollution.

An ‘environmental recovery zone’

According to Carrera, “If this construction is authorized, we will lose what nature took cycles to consolidate.”

She also noted that the land has been subject to various administrative anomalies in recent years, including changes in land-use status by municipal authorities following suspicious fires without observance of the required 20-year waiting period — a timeworn ploy by real estate developers to subvert building restrictions in protected areas, in violation of state-level conservation laws.

Instead, Carrera has called on the State Congress to designate the land as an “environmental recovery zone” and regulate its use to protect the public interest. This legislative proposal arrives at a time when thousands of area residents have filed complaints and grievances over ongoing encroachments to the Primavera Forest.

The fifth annual Grand Book Sale returns to Guadalajara

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Guadalajara Secreta (@guadalajarasecreta)

If you’re a voracious reader who finds the FIL (Guadalajara’s annual International Book Fair) a bit overwhelming and expensive, there’s a lower-profile alternative.

Happening now through Aug. 9, Guadalajara’s Historic Center will be transformed into a gathering place for readers looking to expand their book collections without breaking the bank. The event, which brings together Spanish-language publishers, bookstores and distributors, will feature a wide assortment of books for sale at discounts of 40% or more.

This fifth edition of the book sale (in Spanish, “Magno Remate de Libros”) features 100 booths offering a wide selection of books in various genres, including literature, graphic novels, comics and children’s books. During the 10 days of the sale, there will also be more than 50 literary and cultural activities, including presentations, workshops, author talks, performances and more.

If you’ve been on the hunt for discounted books, this is one of the best opportunities of the year to find new titles at affordable prices.

Dates: July 31 until Aug. 9, 2026. Hours TBD. For more information, visit Cultura Guadalajara’s Instagram.

Location: Paseo Fray Antonio Alcalde, across from Plaza de Armas in Guadalajara’s Historic Center.

Cost: Free and open to the public.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Milei: US Alliance Key to Falklands Sovereignty Claim
World.content:
Politics: Buenos Aires

Key Facts —Statement. President Javier Milei told Radio Mitre on 3 August 2026 that Argentina’s alliance with Washington is the ‘key’ to advancing its claim over the Falklands/Malvinas. —Rationale. Milei argued the United States needs a reliable ally on the Atlantic-to-Pacific passage and that Argentina now meets those conditions. —Caveat. There is no public US statement backing that reading; Washington’s position on the sovereignty dispute has historically been neutral. —Status. The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory; islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain British in 2013, and the UK has administered them since 1833. —Debate. The remarks sharpen a dispute in which a former army chief and other critics say Milei’s approach weakens, rather than strengthens, the claim.

President Javier Milei says Argentina’s alliance with Washington is the ‘key’ to its Falklands (Malvinas) sovereignty claim, a framing that adds a fresh twist to a debate already dividing Buenos Aires.

The Casa Rosada in Buenos Aires. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Milei Puts the US Alliance at the Center

In an interview with Radio Mitre on Monday 3 August 2026, President Javier Milei said his government’s alignment with the United States would allow Argentina to make progress on its sovereignty claim over the Falklands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

‘The United States changed its strategic vision of the world … and it needs a reliable ally on the passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Argentina is meeting all those conditions, and that is the key that will let us recover the Malvinas,’ Milei said, according to MercoPress.

The president called the claim ‘non-negotiable’ and said his government had achieved the greatest diplomatic progress since 1983 toward placing the archipelago, along with South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and surrounding waters, under Argentine administration, a characterisation he attributed to his own record.

What Washington Has Actually Said

There is no public statement from Washington that supports Milei’s interpretation. As MercoPress noted, the US position on the sovereignty dispute has historically been one of neutrality, and no official American declaration has tied the alliance to the Falklands question.

Milei also claimed that ‘for the first time, the UN is forcing England to sit down and talk.’ That assertion is inaccurate. The Decolonization Committee resolutions urging Argentina and the United Kingdom to resume talks are non-binding and have been passed for decades without producing sovereignty negotiations.

The British position has been consistent: London says sovereignty is not in question and that any change would depend on the wishes of the islanders. Reports of a possible review of US neutrality have circulated in the press, but they remain unconfirmed by Washington.

Milei Falklands sovereignty. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The Sea Lion Oil Question

Asked about the Sea Lion oil project, developed by British and Israeli companies in waters near the archipelago that Argentina also claims, Milei said his government had lodged the corresponding diplomatic protests but defended the venture’s private character.

‘We are allies of the United States and Israel, but that is a private company. In a serious country you do not interfere with the private sector,’ he said, according to MercoPress. The first phase of the project reportedly involves investment of around US$1.8 billion and estimated output of more than 170 million barrels.

The exchange underlines the tension in Milei’s position: a maximalist sovereignty claim alongside a hands-off stance toward the commercial activity that Argentina says infringes on it.

Sport, Symbolism and Diplomacy

Milei was also asked about the banner reading ‘Las Malvinas son argentinas’ (the Malvinas are Argentine) displayed by Argentine footballers after a World Cup semifinal against England. He said the episode had not affected dialogue with London, drawing a line between sport and matters of the homeland.

On 29 July, FIFA opened disciplinary proceedings against the Argentine Football Association over messages with political content following the match, part of a wider case tied to conduct after the final whistle.

The president framed the sovereignty push as separate from the sporting flashpoint, arguing that one thing is the sporting question and another the matters linked to the homeland.

A Milei Falklands Sovereignty Stance That Divides Argentina

Milei‘s Falklands sovereignty framing lands in an already polarised debate. Critics at home have argued that his approach, including past comments suggesting he wants islanders to ‘one day vote for us,’ echoes Britain’s emphasis on self-determination and cedes ground rather than pressing the claim.

A former Malvinas secretary and a former army chief have accused the president of weakening Argentina’s historic position, and former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner has gone as far as calling him a ‘traitor.’ Milei’s allies counter that quiet diplomacy and closer ties with Washington are more realistic than decades of confrontation.

What is new in the August remarks is the explicit bet on the US alliance as the decisive lever. Rather than framing the claim primarily around history or the 1982 war, Milei is presenting geopolitics, and Argentina’s usefulness to Washington, as the path forward. That fresh emphasis is what distinguishes this round of comments from earlier exchanges, which you can read alongside The Rio Times’ earlier coverage of the domestic backlash.

What It Means for Expats and Observers

For foreign residents and observers, the dispute is a reminder of how central the Malvinas remain to Argentine politics. The islands sit in the South Atlantic, several hundred kilometres off the Argentine coast, and have been administered by the United Kingdom since 1833.

In a 2013 referendum, Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain a British Overseas Territory. Argentina rejects that vote as a basis for settling sovereignty, and the gap between the two positions has not narrowed.

Whether Milei’s Washington-first strategy yields anything concrete is unproven, and much of his case rests on his own assessment rather than statements from the US or the UK. For now, the practical situation on the islands is unchanged, even as the rhetoric in Buenos Aires sharpens.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Milei say about the Falklands and the United States?

In a Radio Mitre interview on 3 August 2026, President Javier Milei said Argentina’s alliance with Washington is the ‘key’ to advancing its sovereignty claim over the Falklands/Malvinas, arguing the US needs a reliable ally between the Atlantic and Pacific.

Has the United States backed Argentina’s claim?

No. There is no public US statement supporting Milei’s interpretation, and Washington’s position on the sovereignty dispute has historically been neutral. British policy holds that sovereignty is not in question.

Who governs the Falkland Islands?

The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory administered by the United Kingdom since 1833. In a 2013 referendum, islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain British. Argentina maintains a longstanding sovereignty claim.

World.title: Buenos Aires Tango Festival Returns with Free Global Contest
World.content:
Culture: Buenos Aires

Key Facts —Event. The Tango BA Festival y Mundial runs from 20 August to 2 September 2026 at venues across Buenos Aires, with free admission. —Milongas. The eighth Semana de las Milongas opened the city’s Month of Tango from 1 to 7 August 2026 at 59 milongas around the capital. —Venues. Programming spans landmarks including the Teatro Colón, Teatro San Martín, Usina del Arte and Centro Cultural Recoleta. —World championship. The Mundial gathers hundreds of couples from dozens of countries in two categories, Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario. —Access. Entry is free; many shows require advance reservation, and the championship finals are staged at the Teatro Gran Rex.

Buenos Aires turns into the world capital of the 2×4 this August, as the Tango BA Festival y Mundial, the Semana de las Milongas and free shows citywide draw dancers and visitors from dozens of countries.

Tango takes over Buenos Aires each August. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Whole Month Built Around the 2×4

Every August, Buenos Aires devotes itself to tango, and 2026 is no exception. The city’s Month of Tango opened on 1 August with the eighth edition of the Semana de las Milongas, a week of dances, classes and open activities spread across 59 milongas, the social dance halls where the tradition lives night after night.

The week ran from 1 to 7 August and served as a warm-up for the main event. According to the city, the opening took place on Saturday 1 August at the Teatro Verdi, with a milonga that set the tone for the days that followed.

The centrepiece arrives later in the month: the Tango BA Festival y Mundial, which the city’s tourism board lists from 20 August to 2 September 2026. Together, the two programmes turn much of the calendar into a citywide celebration of the genre.

Inside the Festival: Free Shows Across the City

The festival brings together orchestras, ensembles, concerts, staged shows, milongas and special activities. In recent editions the programme has featured well over a thousand artists across dozens of stages, mixing established figures of the genre with younger performers.

Admission is free. For in-person events, some seats are released on a first-come basis, while others must be reserved in advance, typically up to 72 hours before each activity, through the festival’s official channels.

Performances are staged at some of the city’s most recognisable cultural addresses, among them the Teatro Colón, Teatro San Martín, Centro Cultural Recoleta, Usina del Arte and the Centro Cultural 25 de Mayo. The spread of venues is designed to pull tango into neighbourhoods beyond the traditional downtown circuit.

Buenos Aires tango festival. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The Mundial: A World Championship of Tango

The Mundial de Baile is the reason many visitors time their trip for August. Billed as the most important tango dance competition in the world, it brings together couples from dozens of countries who first qualify through preliminary rounds held across Argentina and abroad.

The competition is split into two very different styles. Tango de Pista follows the codes of the social dance floor, prized for its walk, embrace and musicality, while Tango Escenario is a choreographed, theatrical form that allows lifts and dramatic staging.

Coverage of the 2026 edition reported hundreds of couples in the running, with the field narrowing through qualifiers, quarter-finals and semifinals before the grand finals. The finals are traditionally staged at the Teatro Gran Rex, the Avenida Corrientes theatre that seats several thousand.

Where It All Happens

For a first-time visitor, the geography is part of the appeal. The Teatro Colón, one of the world’s great opera houses, anchors the festival’s prestige, while the Usina del Arte, a converted power station in the La Boca district, offers a very different, industrial-era setting.

The Centro Cultural Recoleta, the Teatro San Martín on Avenida Corrientes and the Centro Cultural 25 de Mayo in the Villa Urquiza area extend the map north and west. The milonga circuit, meanwhile, reaches neighbourhood halls that most tourists would never find on their own.

That distribution matters for expats. Rather than a single ticketed arena, the festival is a movable feast, and following it is a way to see parts of Buenos Aires that sit well outside the usual tourist track.

What the Buenos Aires Tango Festival Offers Expats and Visitors

The Buenos Aires tango festival is one of the easiest cultural events for newcomers to join, precisely because it is free and spread across the city. A visitor can watch a world-class final one night and take a beginner class at a milonga the next.

A few practical notes help. August is mid-winter in the Southern Hemisphere, so evenings are cold; many activities require reservations made days ahead; and milonga etiquette, from the cabeceo, the nod used to invite a partner, to the codes of the dance floor, rewards a little homework before you go. Programme details are published on the official site, tangoba.org.

For residents who have long meant to understand tango beyond the tourist shows of San Telmo, the festival is an accessible entry point, with programming pitched at both seasoned dancers and complete beginners.

Why Tango Still Draws the World to Buenos Aires

Tango took shape in the working-class neighbourhoods and port districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late nineteenth century, and it has since become shorthand for the Argentine capital itself. UNESCO added tango to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, a recognition the city leans on heavily.

The ‘2×4’ nickname refers to the music’s characteristic rhythm, and the festival’s mix of live orchestras and social dancing keeps both halves of the tradition, the listening and the dancing, in view. That combination is what sets the Buenos Aires event apart from tango shows staged elsewhere.

For the city, the payoff is more than cultural. The Month of Tango draws international visitors into the low-season winter months, filling milongas, hotels and theatres, and reaffirming the claim that Buenos Aires remains the genre’s global capital.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Tango BA Festival y Mundial 2026?

The Tango BA Festival y Mundial runs from 20 August to 2 September 2026 at venues across Buenos Aires. It is preceded by the Semana de las Milongas, held from 1 to 7 August 2026.

How much do tickets cost?

Admission is free. Some in-person events are first-come, first-served, while others must be reserved in advance, generally up to 72 hours before each activity, through the festival’s official channels.

What is the Mundial de Tango?

The Mundial is a world tango dance championship that brings couples from dozens of countries to compete in two categories, Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario, with the finals staged at the Teatro Gran Rex.

World.title: Guatemala’s Volcán De Fuego Eruption Forces Evacuations
World.content:
Public Safety: Guatemala

Key Facts —Alert. INSIVUMEH says Guatemala’s Volcán de Fuego entered its most explosive ‘paroxysm’ phase late on 3 August 2026, with CONRED coordinating the emergency response. —Timing. The heightened activity could last roughly 24 to 72 hours, according to INSIVUMEH director Edwin Rojas. —Evacuations. Families from the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas hamlets in San Juan Alotenango, Sacatepéquez, are being moved to shelters. —Road closed. Authorities closed National Route 14 (RN-14) at kilometre 83, the entrance to San Juan Alotenango, in both directions. —Hazards. Pyroclastic flows, ash above 7,000 metres and possible lahars threaten communities on the volcano’s west and south flanks.

Guatemala’s Volcán de Fuego eruption has entered a more explosive phase expected to last up to 72 hours, prompting evacuations near San Juan Alotenango and the preventive closure of the road into the town.

Guatemala's Volcán de Fuego during an eruptive phase. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A More Explosive Phase on Fuego

INSIVUMEH, Guatemala’s institute for seismology, volcanology, meteorology and hydrology, reported that the Volcán de Fuego reached its ‘paroxysm’ phase, the moment of greatest eruptive intensity, late on Monday 3 August 2026. The shift was confirmed in special bulletin BEFGO-060-2026 at about 10:35 p.m. local time, roughly 14 hours after the eruptive phase began that morning.

During the peak, the institute recorded a lava fountain rising some 200 to 300 metres above the crater, throwing incandescent material into the upper ravines. INSIVUMEH warned that the eruptive column could climb past 7,000 metres above sea level, feeding a large plume of suspended ash.

INSIVUMEH director Edwin Rojas said that, based on the volcano’s historical behaviour, the heightened activity could last between 24 and 72 hours, though the evolution depends on the volcano itself. It is the first eruptive event of 2026 after a relative lull since June 2025.

Two Villages Evacuated Near Alotenango

The national disaster agency CONRED said it is carrying out preventive evacuations of families from the hamlets of El Porvenir and Las Lajitas, in the municipality of San Juan Alotenango, Sacatepéquez, moving residents to shelters and safe areas while the risk persists.

CONRED executive secretary Claudinne Ogaldes is coordinating prevention and response with the institutions that make up the national disaster system. Spokesperson Valeria Urízar urged residents to rely only on official channels and to follow instructions from the authorities.

San Juan Alotenango sits on the southern side of the volcano, near the colonial tourist city of Antigua Guatemala. The same flanks were devastated by the deadly 2018 eruption, which killed hundreds and remains the reference point for how quickly Fuego’s pyroclastic flows can escalate.

Volcán de Fuego eruption. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The Road Into Alotenango Is Closed

Because of material descending the Las Lajas ravine, authorities ordered the preventive closure of National Route 14 (RN-14) at kilometre 83, the entrance to San Juan Alotenango, and asked people to avoid the sector while the emergency continues.

Road agency PROVIAL said the closure is being maintained in both directions at kilometres 83 and 103 as a safety measure, with crews providing traffic control and operational support in the area.

In a region where RN-14 is a main link between the Pacific lowlands and the highland corridor around Antigua, the closure is a significant disruption. Authorities framed it as a precaution against fast-moving flows rather than a response to any confirmed damage on the road.

Ashfall, Aviation and the Wider Region

INSIVUMEH said ashfall is concentrated on the volcano’s west and southwest flanks, affecting communities in Escuintla, Sacatepéquez and Chimaltenango, particularly San Pedro Yepocapa and its rural villages. Satellite monitoring tracked ash drifting more than 100 kilometres, reaching up to about 130 kilometres to the west.

With ash suspended between roughly 5,000 and 6,000 metres above sea level, the plume also poses a risk to aviation. Guatemala’s civil aviation authority, the DGAC, has issued precautionary recommendations for air navigation in the zone.

Local authorities suspended classes in several municipalities near the volcano and advised residents to wear face masks during ashfall, protect water and food supplies and shelter animals. INSIVUMEH also cautioned about the possibility of lahars, fast flows of hot volcanic material and debris, on the volcano’s slopes.

How Authorities Are Monitoring the Volcano

The head of INSIVUMEH’s volcanology department, Amilcar Roca, said the volcano had not shown a significant increase in activity since June 2025, making this the first eruptive event of 2026. The current episode was detected at around 8:30 a.m. on 3 August.

Monitoring relies on a multi-parameter network of seven stations that combines surveillance cameras, seismic and acoustic sensors, weather stations and satellite data, backed by field observers. INSIVUMEH said the setup lets it follow magma emission, the movement of incandescent material and ash dispersal in real time.

By the time the paroxysm phase was confirmed, INSIVUMEH had issued six special volcanological bulletins and three advisories on ashfall and dispersal. Officials said monitoring would continue around the clock, with new bulletins as the eruption evolves.

What the Volcán de Fuego Eruption Means for Visitors and Expats

For foreign residents and travellers, the practical takeaway is to stay away from the volcano’s flanks and the closed stretch of RN-14, and to check conditions before heading toward Antigua Guatemala or nearby towns. Authorities stressed that the greatest threat remains pyroclastic density currents in the Seca, Taniluyá and Ceniza ravines.

CONRED has repeated its standard guidance to keep a ’72-hour backpack’ ready with documents, water, food and essentials, a reflection of how the agency frames the current window of risk. Residents in exposed communities are asked to be ready to move quickly if instructed.

The situation is fluid, and the most reliable updates come from INSIVUMEH and CONRED rather than social media. For expats across Latin America watching from afar, the episode is a reminder that Fuego, one of Central America’s most active volcanoes, can shift from routine activity to a dangerous phase within hours.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is happening with the Volcán de Fuego right now?

INSIVUMEH says the Volcán de Fuego entered its most explosive ‘paroxysm’ phase late on 3 August 2026, with stronger explosions, pyroclastic flows and heavy ashfall. The institute says the heightened activity could last between 24 and 72 hours.

Which areas have been evacuated or closed?

CONRED is preventively evacuating families from the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas hamlets in San Juan Alotenango, Sacatepéquez. Authorities also closed National Route 14 (RN-14) at kilometre 83, the entrance to Alotenango, in both directions.

Is it safe to travel near Antigua Guatemala?

Authorities urge visitors to avoid the volcano’s flanks and the closed section of RN-14 and to follow INSIVUMEH and CONRED updates. Ashfall is affecting parts of Escuintla, Sacatepéquez and Chimaltenango, and aviation advisories are in place.

World.title: Colombia Presidential Handover Sparks ‘Civil War’ Claim
World.content:
Politics: Colombia

Key Facts —Escalation. Outgoing President Gustavo Petro has intensified his claim that Colombia’s June election was fraudulent and called president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella an “illegitimate” leader. —Allegation. Petro alleges the result was altered by algorithms and foreign intelligence, referencing the United States and Israeli private firms; he has presented no evidence, and authorities and observers reject the claim. —Warning. Petro has said the transfer of power could spark a “civil war,” language his critics call reckless; he has also pledged the handover will proceed under law. —Inauguration. De la Espriella is due to be sworn in on Friday, 7 August 2026, at the Arena USC in Cali — the first presidential inauguration held outside Bogotá. —Guests. Confirmed attendees include FIFA president Gianni Infantino, alongside several regional leaders and foreign dignitaries.

Colombia’s presidential handover has turned combustible, with outgoing President Gustavo Petro branding his successor “illegitimate,” alleging foreign-backed fraud and warning of unrest, days before Friday’s inauguration in Cali.

De la Espriella’s inauguration will be held in Cali, the first outside Bogotá. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

An Already-Tense Transition Escalates

Colombia’s transfer of power has moved from a fractious dispute to the region’s highest-tension political event of the moment. Outgoing President Gustavo Petro has sharpened his rejection of the June election result, calling president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella an “illegitimate” president days before the handover.

The Rio Times has previously reported that Petro said he would not attend the inauguration, citing his fraud claims. What is new is the intensity: Petro has now paired that boycott with a warning that the transition could, in his words, trigger a “civil war.”

Petro has also said the handover will nonetheless proceed by law until his term ends, a message his office has repeated even as his rhetoric hardens.

The Fraud Allegation, and Who Rejects It

Petro claims the vote was altered after ballots were counted, alleging that security codes on tally sheets were stripped so results could be manipulated. He has attributed the operation to “algorithms from California” run by what he called Israeli private-intelligence firms, financed with illicit money — language invoking the United States and Israel.

He maintains the true winner was his ally Iván Cepeda. Petro has not presented evidence to judicial authorities to support the accusations, which are extraordinary in their scope.

Colombia’s electoral authorities — the National Civil Registry and the National Electoral Council — and international observers have rejected the fraud claims, and electoral judges have certified the result.

Colombia presidential handover. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What the Numbers Show

According to Colombia’s official results, De la Espriella won the 21 June runoff with about 12.96 million votes (49.66%) to roughly 12.71 million (48.70%) for Cepeda, a margin of some 250,000 votes. It was one of the closest presidential contests in recent Colombian history.

The narrowness of the result is part of what has fueled the dispute, giving Petro’s allegations political resonance even as institutions dismiss them on the evidence.

Analysts note that a contested-but-certified result can strain a new government’s legitimacy in the eyes of some voters, deepening polarization regardless of the courts’ rulings.

A First-Ever Inauguration in Cali

In a break with tradition, De la Espriella is set to be sworn in on Friday, 7 August 2026, at the Arena USC in Cali rather than in Bogotá — the first Colombian presidential inauguration held outside the capital. The move followed a dispute over the venue, after Petro objected to holding the ceremony at a military site.

Cali, one of Colombia’s largest cities, will host heavy security for the event. Both chambers of Congress signed off on the location.

The choice adds symbolic weight to an already charged handover, shifting the country’s marquee political ritual away from its historic seat of power.

Infantino and a Watchful Region

The guest list has drawn attention beyond politics: FIFA president Gianni Infantino is expected to attend, alongside regional leaders and foreign dignitaries. His presence underscores the international profile of the event and Colombia’s ties to global football.

Investors, meanwhile, are watching the Colombian peso and local markets for any sign that the political friction spills into economic confidence. Heightened uncertainty around a leadership transition can weigh on currencies, though the handover is proceeding within the constitutional timeline.

For foreign residents and businesses, the immediate takeaway is that the ceremony is expected to go ahead on schedule, even as the rhetoric surrounding it remains unusually heated. Readers can follow The Rio Times’ earlier coverage of Petro’s decision to skip the event for how the standoff developed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Petro call the incoming president illegitimate?

Petro alleges the June 2026 election was defrauded and says the real winner was his ally Iván Cepeda. He has offered no evidence to courts, and Colombia’s electoral authorities and international observers have rejected the claim and certified De la Espriella’s win.

When and where is the inauguration?

Abelardo de la Espriella is scheduled to be inaugurated on Friday, 7 August 2026, at the Arena USC in Cali — the first Colombian presidential inauguration held outside Bogotá.

Is FIFA’s Gianni Infantino attending?

FIFA president Gianni Infantino is among the confirmed guests for the ceremony, alongside several regional leaders and foreign dignitaries.

World.title: Guatemala Ports Law Vote Set for August as US Demands Reform
World.content:
Trade: Guatemala

Key Facts —Bill. Guatemala’s General Ports System Law reached the plenary of Congress for a possible vote around 4 August 2026, after months of negotiation. —Amendments. Bloc leaders agreed on a package of about 36 amendments; earlier counts cited 32 to 33 before a late change to the sector’s governing board. —Purpose. The bill would create a single national framework for port infrastructure, replacing a patchwork of bodies, as demand outstrips current capacity. —US position. The United States said such a law would be a “decisive step” to boost Guatemala’s competitiveness, deepen trade with Washington and spread prosperity in the region. —Stakes. Guatemalan ports handled about 9.2 million tonnes and 504,000 containers in 2024, trade worth roughly US$7.8 billion.

Guatemala’s ports law reached the plenary of Congress with about 36 negotiated amendments, and the United States is publicly urging lawmakers to pass it to strengthen trade and investment.

Guatemala’s congress is debating a new ports law to modernize the country’s harbors. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Long-Delayed Ports Reform Reaches the Floor

Guatemala’s Congress moved the General Ports System Law (Ley General del Sistema Portuario Nacional) to the plenary for a possible vote in early August 2026, after bloc leaders spent weeks negotiating changes to the text. Lawmakers had signaled they hoped to approve it during the session.

The initiative aims to give the country a single legal framework for developing its commercial ports, which supporters say have run up against capacity limits. Guatemala currently lacks one general law concentrating regulation of the port system, relying instead on a mix of separate bodies.

For foreign investors and traders, the vote matters because ports are the physical backbone of Guatemala’s export economy and a bottleneck when cargo volumes rise.

What the Roughly 36 Amendments Cover

According to Guatemalan media, the leaders of congressional blocs agreed on a package of about 36 amendments before sending the bill to the floor. Earlier in the process, negotiators had cited 32 to 33 consensus changes, with the count rising after a late proposal to alter the composition of the sector’s governing board.

The head of the Economy and Foreign Trade Commission, Jorge Ayala, said the amendments had been reviewed and agreed on technical grounds. Prior versions of the reform had stalled over dozens of pending amendments tied to port-security rules and union concerns.

The negotiated package is meant to clear those objections and assemble the votes needed for passage.

Guatemala ports law. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Why Washington Is Weighing In

In an unusual public intervention, the United States urged Guatemala to advance the ports law. A law of this type, Washington said, would represent a “decisive step to increase Guatemala’s competitiveness, deepen trade with the United States and generate prosperity throughout the region.”

The statement fits a broader US push to strengthen commercial ties and supply chains in Central America. Guatemala sends coffee, bananas, sugar, apparel and textiles to the US market, and modern port infrastructure affects the cost and reliability of those flows.

US backing gives domestic supporters of the bill an external argument, though port reform remains a decision for Guatemala’s Congress alone.

What the Law Would Change

Earlier drafts of the reform would replace decades-old port arrangements with a single national authority to plan and regulate the sector, and would let private operators run terminals under long-term concessions to attract large-scale investment. The version reaching the floor reflects months of amendment.

Backers argue that clearer rules and longer concession horizons are needed to fund upgrades at ports that are struggling to keep pace with trade. Critics have raised concerns about security oversight and labor protections, some of which the amendments seek to address.

The exact final shape of the authority and the concession terms will depend on the text lawmakers ultimately approve.

The Trade and Investment Stakes

Guatemalan ports moved about 9.2 million tonnes of cargo and 504,000 containers in 2024, a flow worth roughly US$7.8 billion, underscoring how central they are to the economy. Congestion at the busiest Pacific harbor has added urgency to the reform.

A functioning ports law could unlock private capital for terminals and equipment, potentially easing delays that raise costs for importers and exporters. That prospect is what draws the interest of investors and trade partners, including the United States.

For expats and foreign businesses across the region, the outcome is a test of whether Guatemala can convert political consensus into infrastructure that keeps its trade competitive. The Rio Times has tracked the reform’s earlier stall amid congestion at Puerto Quetzal.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Guatemala’s ports law?

It is the General Ports System Law, a bill to create a single national framework for regulating and developing Guatemala’s commercial ports, replacing a patchwork of separate bodies as cargo demand outpaces capacity.

How many amendments does the bill have?

Congressional bloc leaders agreed on a package of about 36 amendments before sending the bill to the plenary; earlier stages of the process cited 32 to 33 consensus changes.

Why does the United States support the law?

Washington said such a law would be a “decisive step” to increase Guatemala’s competitiveness, deepen trade with the United States and generate prosperity across the region.

World.title: Peru’s Ex-President Toledo, 80, Seeks Prison Release over Health
World.content:
Politics: Peru

Key Facts —Request. Alejandro Toledo, who governed Peru from 2001 to 2006, has asked to be released from prison on humanitarian grounds, citing his age and deteriorating health, according to his lawyer. —Mechanism. His defense filed for a presidential grace (gracia presidencial) and is also weighing a 2025 humanitarian law allowing house arrest for inmates over 80. —Health claim. Toledo, now 80, says his condition has worsened in custody; his team says doctors have warned of a possible heart attack or stroke. These claims have not been independently verified. —Status. He has been held at Lima’s Barbadillo prison since 2023, when the United States extradited him to Peru. —Sentence. In 2024 a court sentenced him to 20 years and six months in the Odebrecht case; he has denied wrongdoing.

Alejandro Toledo, Peru’s president from 2001 to 2006, is seeking release from prison on health grounds, asking for a humanitarian presidential grace as he serves a 20-year sentence in the Odebrecht corruption case.

Peru’s justice system is weighing former president Alejandro Toledo’s request for release. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What Toledo Is Asking For

Through his lawyer, former president Alejandro Toledo has requested to leave prison on humanitarian grounds, arguing that his advanced age and failing health make continued detention a threat to his life. He has said he does not want to die behind bars.

The petition centers on a “presidential grace” (gracia presidencial), a clemency mechanism handled by Peru’s executive branch. His defense has also signaled it may invoke a 2025 humanitarian law that allows inmates over the age of 80 to serve their sentences under house arrest.

Peruvian media reported that the request was addressed to the head of state and forwarded to the Justice Ministry’s Presidential Pardons Commission, which reviews such cases before any decision is made.

The Health Claims at the Center of the Request

Toledo, now 80, says his health has deteriorated significantly since he entered prison. According to statements from his legal team, doctors have warned that he could suffer a heart attack or stroke, and he has described serious cardiac problems and other ailments.

These are claims made by Toledo and his defense; they have not been independently confirmed by prison or health authorities, and any grace request would typically require a technical and medical evaluation before it advances.

For readers following Latin American politics, humanitarian clemency for convicted former leaders is a recurring and often contentious issue, weighing an inmate’s health against public demands for accountability.

Alejandro Toledo release from prison. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

How Toledo Ended Up in Barbadillo Prison

Toledo has been held at the Barbadillo penitentiary in Lima since 2023, when the United States extradited him after years of legal battles in California. The facility has become notable for housing several of Peru’s former presidents at the same time.

An economist with a doctorate from Stanford University, Toledo led Peru during a period of economic growth in the early 2000s. His fall came through the sprawling Odebrecht scandal, which implicated politicians across Latin America.

The case turned on allegations that he accepted about US$35 million in bribes from the Brazilian construction giant in exchange for public-works contracts during his term.

The Sentences He Is Serving

In 2024, a Peruvian court sentenced Toledo to 20 years and six months in prison in the Odebrecht case, finding him responsible for aggravated collusion and money laundering. He has denied wrongdoing throughout the proceedings.

In a separate matter known as the Ecoteva case, he received an additional sentence of 13 years and four months for money laundering. Together, the rulings would keep him incarcerated well beyond his current age.

Because the convictions stand in the courts that issued them, a humanitarian grace or house-arrest arrangement is one of the few remaining routes his defense can pursue to secure his release.

What Happens Next

The decision on a presidential grace ultimately rests with Peru’s president, acting on the recommendation of the Pardons Commission after its technical and medical review. There is no fixed timetable for such a ruling.

The request lands amid an unusually turbulent period in Peruvian politics, with rapid turnover at the top of government and several former presidents facing prosecution or imprisonment. Any move to release Toledo would be closely scrutinized.

For now, Toledo remains in Barbadillo, and his petition adds to a broader regional debate over how democracies handle aging, ailing leaders convicted of corruption.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Alejandro Toledo asking for?

Toledo is asking to be released from prison on humanitarian grounds, citing his age and health. His defense has requested a presidential grace and may also invoke a 2025 law allowing house arrest for inmates over 80.

What was Alejandro Toledo convicted of?

In 2024 a Peruvian court sentenced him to 20 years and six months in the Odebrecht case for aggravated collusion and money laundering, tied to allegations he took about US$35 million in bribes. He received a further term in the separate Ecoteva case and has denied wrongdoing.

Where is Toledo being held?

He has been detained at Lima’s Barbadillo prison since 2023, when the United States extradited him to Peru. The prison also holds other former Peruvian presidents.

World.title: Argentina’s Dividend Payments Abroad Top US$1 Billion in June
World.content:
Economy: Argentina

Key Facts —Figure. In June 2026, companies transferred about US$1.023 billion abroad in profits and dividends, according to the central bank’s foreign-exchange balance — the largest monthly outflow since 2010. —Sectors. Energy (US$165 million), food, beverages and tobacco (US$135 million), mining (US$125 million) and financial firms (US$112 million) together made up more than half the total. —Rule change. The transfers follow Communication “A” 8226, in force since April 2025, which lets firms remit profits earned in fiscal years starting on or after 1 January 2025. —Dollar demand. The outflow was a leading source of dollar demand in June and helped narrow the current-account surplus from about US$1.877 billion to US$857 million. —Reserves. Gross central-bank reserves fell roughly US$3.323 billion in June, though they still rose about US$3.775 billion across the first half of 2026.

Argentine companies’ dividend payments abroad topped US$1 billion in June 2026 — the most in any single month since 2010 — as firms accelerated profit transfers after the government eased currency controls.

Argentina’s central bank tracks dividend payments abroad in its foreign-exchange balance. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)
