Tech.title: Is This Poker Player Bluffing? The AI Thinks So
Tech.content:
For serious poker players, the ability to sniff out the “tells” that expose an opponent’s intentions is nearly as important to winning as the cards themselves.

Many gamblers have made careers out of their ability to decipher the meaning of everything other players do at the table—their conscious movements, their body language, and their subconscious tics, all of which might reveal their strategy—as a method of gaining an edge in this game of incomplete information.

It’s understandable, then, that ESPN’s use of a new “AI tells detection” tool during the 2026 World Series of Poker Main Event broadcast stoked some serious debate within the poker community.

The tool began appearing periodically during the first few days of the tournament’s live broadcast in early July. A text overlay displayed various live metrics on a player’s movements, plus a “hand strength model” chart breaking down different possibilities of the type of hand a player might be holding. The tool looks slick, but a viewer might naturally wonder how accurate its data is, or how the AI came to know the players’ tics and gestures well enough to venture such a guess.

Is the tool just a neat party trick—or a silly one, depending on your sensibilities? Or is it an attempt to haphazardly stuff AI into the inherently human pursuit of poker, threatening the game’s soul and future?

Do Tell

Hundreds of pros on the poker circuit specialize in spotting tells. This new tool, designed by an AI engineer for the US Air Force named Luke Geel, purports to digitize that process. It’s watched every hand captured on camera in the 2026 WSOP Main Event to build a tells database on various players.

The system gathers inputs on the players ranging from eye movements and the rate at which they blink, to the players’ posture, chip handling movements, “hand fidget” metrics, and more. It analyzes that data and the outcomes of each hand to predict the likelihood of which general hand type a player might have: A strong made hand, a drawing hand, a bluff, and so on.

The poker experts I spoke to are skeptical about the tool’s effectiveness—especially since it was trained on such a small amount of data. The 2026 edition of the WSOP Main Event tournament drew over 9,000 entries, but the vast majority of those players never spent time at one of three tables that were being recorded by cameras. (The same camera feeds used for the broadcast were also used to train the AI tool). Even those who did sit at those tables weren’t there long enough for the system to build a robust dataset that covers the vast range of situations possible in poker.

Tech.title: How One Startup Built a (Mostly) China-Free Robot
Tech.content:
Last week, US regulators banned a wide variety of Chinese-made robots from being imported to the United States because of concerns about national security. Saurabh Chandra was ready to seize the moment. His company, Ati Robotics, assembles its robots in India, and Chandra believes they use fewer Chinese parts than almost any other robotics company in the US.

Investment in robotics startups hit record highs this year, both in the number of deals and dollars invested, according to PitchBook, which tracks venture capital flows. But many of those companies primarily develop software, and they largely still rely on Chinese suppliers for their hardware.

The Federal Communications Commission’s decision to ban new models of human-like robots, known as humanoids, and other advanced devices from China could hamper the growth of many smaller robotics firms in the US. But some businesses could benefit, including Ati.

The startup was founded in 2017 to develop motors for self-driving cars. Years later, it zeroed in on making its own robots, including tuggers and pallet movers that cart tons of materials throughout big facilities. Ati developed its own hardware, believing that it would lead to better functionality, a bet that Chandra says many of his advisers cautioned against but one that wound up naturally limiting reliance on China.

It has begun to pay off. Ati has several hundred robots currently in operation at warehouses and factories and more than 50 customers in total, Chandra says. Ati’s first humanoid, which moves heavy bins around, will go into service later this year.

Chandra spoke with WIRED last week about how Ati Robotics steered clear of China, while building robots he argues can still compete with the industry’s best on price and performance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

WIRED: Developing hardware is expensive. How were you able to financially sustain doing that?

Saurabh Chandra: R&D is in Bangalore, which helps with our labor costs. Bangalore was undergoing this electric vehicle revolution in the two-wheeler, three-wheeler category in India. And it turns out that the kind of vehicles we were making for the robotics industry happened to have a similar power profile and characteristic as the two-wheeler and three-wheelers being made in the EV industry.

We tried to leverage the components and supply chain being developed for those vehicles. Typically, automotive parts are very reliable and are produced in large volumes, hence they are very good and cost-efficient. Though we had to do engineering with some of those vendors to make the parts work in a robot. But once we did, we had a great win.

One of your robot models is China-free, right, but not the others?

They have different levels of what I might call “supply chain resiliency.” Two of our best-selling models—our 10,000-pound tugger and the pallet mover—use very few parts from China. They're tugging trolleys—you may be taking raw material from stores to the factory line or from one process point to another.

But even with the humanoid that we have, the full arm is done here in Bangalore. The actuator is also done here, but we do get the harmonic drive from China, for example, and the frameless motor, at least for now.

The battery cells come from China. But we could, for example, get the cells from South Korea or Japan tomorrow. So those are passive components. There are some components that do come from China when we go deeper. We use induction motors, so even the magnet in the motor is not coming from China. That’s a very different choice from many of the people who are doing robots.

Tech.title: ‘Everyone Is Doing It’: The Truth About AI in Hollywood
Tech.content:
If you want a clear understanding of how AI is affecting Hollywood … good luck.

Some of the industry loathes the technology, with screenwriters, directors, and actors alike vowing never to use AI in their work—or collaborate with those who do. Others are much more open to the potential for AI to act as everything from creative partner to cost-cutting engine. And a rare few, Ben Affleck included, are already making millions by capitalizing on AI’s nascent potential to (they argue) streamline and improve the filmmaking process.

At WIRED, we’re constantly doing our best to document AI’s transformational effects on the entertainment business, for better and for worse. (If you haven’t read Ruth Fowler’s recent essay for us, on going from a screenwriter to an underemployed LLM trainer, I highly recommend it.) But in an effort to get the most nuanced possible view, I wanted to talk to someone who knows the industry and its players inside and out.

Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck, has covered Hollywood for decades. He writes a scoopy newsletter (What I’m Hearing …) and hosts a scoopy podcast (The Town) that frequently focus on AI and Big Tech as both become increasingly dominant forces across entertainment. Belloni also happens to be a former lawyer, making him the ideal person to ask about the ongoing, and highly consequential, debates over AI and copyright, IP, and celebrity likeness.

Belloni was generous enough to give me an hour of his time, and we managed to cover all the bases—from whether Hollywood types side-eyed Ben Affleck after he sold an AI startup to Netflix for $587 million, to just how much control Big Tech companies now wield over the entertainment industry. You can read our conversation above or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Matt, I have to start with the obvious, which is artificial intelligence. You've been on top of AI in Hollywood for a very long time, and you've said multiple times that, quote, “everyone is doing it,” meaning everyone [in the industry] is using AI. What exactly do you mean by that?

MATTHEW BELLONI: Well, there's two types of AI, as you know. There's generative AI, which is content creation and things like that, and then there's what I refer to as the corporate AI, like streamlining processes and better search results. Obviously, on the second one, everyone is using it.

I'm not going to name a name, but I heard a very interesting story about a very prominent showrunner who went into the writer's room and basically castigated her writing team for not using ChatGPT to help with the process.

To help with the creative process? Or the admin and bookkeeping?

The creative process. Here's a scenario, suggest some jokes. Here's this, this, this. It doesn't mean they use them. You could do the same thing with Google. It's just better, and people are using it. I know, I've talked to screenwriters who use it to suggest scenarios or to give a description of the inside of a building where they want a scenario to play out, or things that to me seem like part of the process.

You may not know this, but the Writers Guild is actually OK with that. As long as there is a credited writer on every script and that this process doesn't impact jobs, they're OK with the use of this technology.

That's one side. Then the other side is generative and how this is making content. There it's a little murkier, because there are a lot of studios that are purporting to create AI-generated movies, shorts, TV pilots. I've seen a lot of them. They're not great. They're better in animation, and I think this is where we're going to see the disruption first, but you can always kinda tell, and that's the problem when you're trying to relate to people. I can't wait to see what Elon's historically accurate version of The Odyssey looks like.

Tech.title: How Data Centers Broke American Politics
Tech.content:
Joe Allen wants to know what the robot’s name is. At first, I think the double whiskey we downed at the hotel bar must be getting to him, as he sprints like a kid at recess toward a delivery vehicle. I’m anxious about the time: I’m supposed to be driving Allen to the airport, my Hail Mary effort to get him alone for a proper conversation before he leaves Atlanta.

I’ve been back and forth with Allen, who rose to national prominence as the anti-tech prophet on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast, for a few weeks now, seeking an entry into the growing movement against AI. I’d come down to Georgia, a hot spot of data center resistance, to hear one of Allen’s lectures, which he’s been giving at locations across the country. But when I got to the event, he told me he had to leave immediately after.

Fortunately, his flight keeps getting pushed back, which means I can follow him around on various side quests—like this one, to meet some friends at a nearby restaurant. He manages to evade most of my questions about their identities, changing the topic to more interesting things, like the “inverse singularity” (his idea that humanity will approach a point where our intellect and creativity collapse as we rely increasingly on AI for information). Allen’s friends at the restaurant have similarly little information about me, it seems. On our way, one of them calls Allen to ask for an ETA. “I’m bringing a friend—well, a frenemy,” he says, giving me a dramatic side-eye.

There are delivery robots all over downtown Atlanta, one of a handful of major metropolitan areas where they’re being rolled out to bring people burgers or tacos. Allen catches up to this one—which, I’m alarmed to see, has luminous white lights shaped like eyes on its front—and reads a name off the side: “CJ.” I think of the title of Allen’s recent book, Dark Aeon: Transhumanism and the War Against Humanity, and wonder what happened to the delivery worker that this robot replaced. Its eyes look pathetically, limply, past me.

When people ask what I’m doing in Georgia, I give them something easy. People hate data centers, I say, so I’m trying to figure out if they hate AI too. That’s all true. But the topic has also consumed me. In all my years of reporting on energy and the environment, I have never seen anything like the type of vitriol leveled at data centers, or the near-religious fury that has built up around their construction, or the way this resistance seems to be uniting people from the complete opposite ends of the political spectrum.

As I’m writing this piece, a friend sends me a post from a “white Christian nationalism” account on X: a seemingly AI-generated cartoon of Smokey Bear standing in front of a burning data-center-like structure, with the text “ONLY YOU CAN PREVENT DATA CENTERS.” What is happening? my friend asks. I’ll try to explain.

Once upon a time, you may have been living next to a data center and never heard anything about it.

For the past few decades, data centers have been quietly built all over the US, largely in areas with both fiber connectivity and proximity to power—Silicon Valley and the DC area were popular choices. They helped stream Netflix or store stuff in the cloud or do any one of the countless stupid and important things we all do constantly online.

Tech.title: The EPA Cut Short a Gas Stove Study — the Results Are Alarming
Tech.content:
A study cut short by the Trump administration suggests gas stoves may worsen asthma symptoms. Tyler Lizenby/CNET

A study published in July examined the health effects of gas stoves and the results show an alarming connection between gas-powered cooking and asthma symptoms.

Conducted by MetroHealth System — a Northeast Ohio hospital and academic medical center — in collaboration with six community organizations, the research found that participants with asthma reported improvements in symptoms after switching from gas to electric.

The study was funded for three years by the US Environmental Protection Agency starting in late 2024, but was terminated by the Trump administration in May of 2025.

According to one researcher, Dr. Ashwini Sehgal, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, this is the first study to explore whether switching from a gas to an electric stove can reduce asthma symptoms.

What the study found

Participants reported improved asthma symptoms after having their gas stoves swapped for electric. Alessandro Citterio/CNET

The study included 85 adults and children in Northeast Ohio with “poorly controlled asthma,” which was based on their symptoms, use of emergency medication and activity limitations. Each participant logged this information not only one to four weeks before their gas stoves were replaced at no cost with electric induction models, but also two to three months after the replacement.

“We chose electric induction stoves because they heat up and cool down rapidly, and they are safer and easier to clean than electric coil stoves,” Sehgal wrote in his The Conversation article. While induction stoves use an electromagnetic field to heat your cookware, electric stoves rely on electricity to do so.

Before and after the stoves were replaced, air quality monitors were used to measure nitrogen dioxide levels for seven-day periods. Nitrogen dioxide, a gaseous air pollutant emitted by gas stoves, can harm the lungs.

After the switch from gas to electric, indoor nitrogen dioxide levels decreased by 70%, and according to Sehgal, participants’ asthma symptoms went from moderate to mild, demonstrating improvements “similar to — or even greater than — those reported in clinical trials of commonly used asthma medications.”

Missed days of work or school decreased by about 80%, while ER visits and hospitalizations decreased by 70%.

Aside from asthma improvement, 98% of participants reported feeling satisfied or very satisfied with their new electric induction stoves, whereas 41% felt the same about their previous gas models.

An induction stove uses electricity, not gas, to work. Juan Algar/Getty Images

The study’s limitations

Sehgal notes that the study followed only a small number of people for a few months and did not include a comparison group with gas stoves. The results were also based on a self-reported questionnaire rather than medical records.

Results may not apply to people with mild asthma or to other US regions with different nitrogen dioxide levels.

Information wasn’t collected on other household sources of nitrogen dioxide, such as fireplaces or kerosene heaters, nor was data on participants’ allergy status, stove usage or additional medications.

As a result, further research is needed to confirm the study’s findings and to better understand long-term outcomes.

Researchers weren’t able to increase the study’s sample size or duration because the Trump administration terminated the project in May 2025, after it was selected for three years of funding by the EPA in December 2024.

Important considerations

As Sehgal put it in his article, switching from a gas stove to an electric one will not cure asthma or serve as a replacement for medical care and other health precautions.

It should also be considered that replacing a stove may not be financially feasible for many. “Most of our study participants lived in homes that were built before 1960, and we spent an average of $7,000 per household to upgrade their electrical systems as part of the study,” wrote Sehgal, adding that an electric stove plus installation costs about $1,500 in newer US homes.

If you have a gas stove, make sure you use the range hood’s exhaust fan to reduce airborne pollutants inside your home. Nattawat Jindamaneesirikul/Getty Images

What other stove research shows

Gas stoves are a source of indoor air pollution, as they emit gaseous pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds such as benzene and formaldehyde, both of which can cause cancer.

A May 2024 study found that nitrogen dioxide, in particular, is produced by gas stoves in the US at short-term exposure levels higher than those deemed safe by both the US Environmental Protection Agency and the World Health Organization.

The 2024 study also estimated that, at the time, 50,000 cases of childhood asthma were linked to nitrogen dioxide emitted by gas stoves. If other gas stove pollutants were included, that number could rise to about 200,000 cases. Nitrogen dioxide has also been connected to lung cancer, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and preterm birth.

Along with increased levels of particulate matter and sulfur dioxide, the American Lung Association reports that nitrogen dioxide has been linked to cancer, autoimmune disorders, pregnancy and birth outcomes and harm to the heart, lungs, kidneys and nervous system.

The University of California, Davis, Environmental Health Science Center adds that both electric and gas cooking can release PM2.5 (particles with a diameter of 2.5 microns or less) and ultrafine particles, which can cause or worsen respiratory conditions and increase the risk for cardiovascular disease, neurological disorders and immune system dysfunction.

In fact, frying foods on electric stoves produced higher particulate matter levels than on gas stoves.

However, it should be noted that gas stove pollutant levels can vary from home to home and that health effects will depend on these levels and the length of exposure. One’s lifestyle, health, age and current medical conditions can also determine health effects.

How to reduce indoor cooking air pollution

If you’re unable to switch from a gas to an electric stove, you can take other steps to reduce indoor air pollution when cooking. When outdoor air pollution is low, increase ventilation by opening windows and using your range hood’s exhaust.

If that isn’t feasible, consider purchasing an air purifier for your kitchen, which can filter out cooking particles and, if it includes an activated carbon filter, some gases, such as VOCs. Just make sure you regularly replace your air purifier’s filter so it works as intended, as it can spit pollutants back into your home if it becomes saturated.

At the end of the day, while replacing your gas stove with an electric model can reduce indoor air pollution and its health effects, it isn’t a complete solution. There are other steps you can take to improve your air quality.

Tech.title: Signalis and Dying Light 2 Dominate PlayStation Plus’s Free Games This Month
Tech.content:
Sony last week announced the next batch of PlayStation Plus monthly games for August, and these games confirm for me that gaming inside to beat the heat all summer was one of my better ideas. People online rave about Signalis, and Dying Light 2 has generally favorable reviews on Metacritic. Big Walk seems like a fun, cartoony co-op game that many people should enjoy for its silliness and puzzles. And all PlayStation Plus subscribers can play these games now until the end of August.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 per month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge.

If you subscribe to PlayStation Plus, here are the games you can play at no additional cost now until Aug. 31.

Signalis

Some folks on Reddit call this game a “Resident Evil game that’s secretly a Silent Hill game that’s actually a love story,” which should pique the interest of many horror game enthusiasts. You play as Elster, a humanoid android called a Replika, who is searching for her lost partner and missing dreams in a dystopian solar system. You’ll explore a derelict spaceship, fight nightmarish creatures and solve puzzles along the way with limited resources. Maybe play this survival horror game with the lights on.

Dying Light 2 Stay Human: Reloaded Edition

This game takes place about 20 years after the original and – spoiler – the virus that turns people into zombies has nearly won. You play as one of the last survivors, who is tasked with delivering goods and news between settlements. But really, you’re looking for your sister in all the chaos. The only issue is you’ve got hordes of zombies to get through. Use parkour and brutal weapons to get through the undead and survive another day.

Big Walk

This goofy-looking game from the makers of Untitled Goose Game is all about solving puzzles, cooperation and talking. Set off with your friends in a wide world filled with puzzles and adventure, and that’s just half the fun. The other half is hanging out with your pals as you all watch a sunset, or stealing your friends’ binoculars and kicking them over a cliff. It’s all in good fun.

For more on PlayStation Plus, here’s what to know about the gaming service and a rundown of PS Plus Extra and Premium games added in July. You can also check out the latest and upcoming games on Xbox Game Pass.

Tech.title: Flock’s AI Cameras May Have Misread Over 70% of License Plates, Creating New Headaches for Cities
Tech.content:
Flock Safety can’t seem to stay out of the news recently, from the latest wave of attacks on Flock surveillance cameras to claims that Flock’s gunshot detection microphones are also picking up private home conversations. But one specific report has caught my attention — a study showing a startlingly high failure rate for the surveillance system AI.



Following up on complaints about Flock Safety flagging vehicles incorrectly, the police department of Roseville, California, ran its own analysis of the cameras, studying nearly 1,500 Flock reports. They found an astonishing 71% failure rate, where the cameras would mistake one license plate number for another.

That’s not just a snafu. Mistaking one number for another, like seeing a 7 as a 1, can lead Flock cameras to incorrectly identify an innocent vehicle as one that was previously stolen. That’s exactly what happened in the California situation, where a citizen complained that the cameras were repeatedly flagging his car to police as stolen because the AI technology interpreted a 9 as an 8.

This is a stark contrast to Flock’s own claims — sort of. The company reports that independent evaluations show its cameras have a 96% vehicle count accuracy rating, while correctly categorizing 92% into vehicle types. But accurately recognizing vehicles is a far cry from accurately reading license plates, which Flock doesn’t provide much data on. I’ve reached out to Flock to learn more, and I’ll let you know if the company has additional details to provide.

Why this Flock failure rate could cause trouble

If Flock camera accuracy isn’t reliable, what reason do cities have to use them? Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

It’s important to note that this analysis was conducted between 2023 and 2024. Many AI Large Language Models can improve over time with better training and more access to material, which is one reason AI companies are literally devouring old books these days. So Flock’s cameras may have improved in accuracy by now. However, we’ve also seen the opposite happen: AI models can eat up bad data, especially “recursive” data that was created by another AI, and start becoming dumber, less accurate when performing their tasks.

Flock has said that the camera setup Roseville used wasn’t typical, but didn’t provide more details. It’s possible that where cameras are placed and when they are activated (at night, in the rain, etc.) can have a significant impact on accuracy. So can license plate covers, dirty license plates and unusual license plate placement.

The problem is these are issues any city may face when adopting Flock cameras. Flock’s primary value offering is that the company’s surveillance is ubiquitous, speedy and accurate, doing a job that police can’t. But if the cameras make mistakes when encountering everyday situations, that’s more work for law enforcement, not less.

Cities, including Los Angeles, continue to cancel Flock contracts (although sometimes they just switch to another provider), often due to public pressure. If Flock’s core services could have such a high failure rate, that’s another reason for police and sheriff departments to reconsider their use, and could make it difficult for Flock to sell new cities on its technology.

Tech.title: T-Mobile Is Stretching Its Device Commitment to 3 Years with New Installment and ‘2.0’ Phone Plans
Tech.content:
In an environment in which everything costs more, the major wireless phone carriers have introduced plans to draw in customers who want to reduce what millions of people see as an essential expense. In recent months, AT&T introduced its modular Build-A-Plan, and Verizon cut prices and then rolled out its Simplicity plan.

Now it’s T-Mobile’s turn.

Starting Thursday, the company is adding a new installment plan for phone purchases, rebranding its slate of unlimited wireless plans and offering student plans with the option to add 5G home internet service.

An extended phone flex

Currently, when you purchase a new phone through T-Mobile, you can buy it outright or pay a monthly installment over 24 months. The new Equipment Installment Plan Flex 36 option lets you make those payments over 36 months, reducing the monthly amount.

What makes EIP Flex 36 different from the company’s EIP Standard plan (which remains an option as EIP Standard 36) is that all upfront costs are rolled into those three years of payments — the device, taxes and fees — making the initial cost zero. Even with most zero percent finance plans, customers must pay taxes on the cost of the phone and pay an activation fee.

T-Mobile’s press release says the EIP Flex 36 option for “well-qualified customers” has, “for a limited time, 0% APR.” It’s not clear if that means interest will go up sometime during the life of the installment plan; when I reached out to a T-Mobile representative for clarification, they reiterated the reduced monthly payments but did not define the timeline of when interest might kick in.

Going forward, the financing options for new customers will be to choose a 36-month EIP plan or pay the full cost of the device. If you want to pay off a phone earlier than the full term, that’s an option, too.

‘2.0’”’ unlimited plans (that feel more like 1.1)

In software, a full-number version increment implies an update that’s bigger than small tweaks; it’s why your iPhone was recently updated to iOS 26.6, applying fixes and security updates, while iOS 27.0 was just released in beta, with major new features — such as Siri AI — and is expected in September.

Along with EIP Flex 36, T-Mobile is updating its unlimited postpaid mobile plans to 2.0 versions: Experience Beyond 2.0, Experience More 2.0 and Essentials 2.0. (The company did not specifically call out the budget Essentials Saver plan, but I’m told that it will also get the 2.0 treatment.)

However, the 2.0 in this case appears to be a formality to pair with the EIP Flex 36 and EIP Standard 36 installment plans: The features and base pricing remain the same as the Experience Beyond, Experience More and Essentials plans.

T-Mobile says that customers already on those plans can stay where they are, or switch to the 2.0 versions if they want to take advantage of the 36-month financing option.

Student Perks plans

Now that it’s August, with the academic year about to begin, college-bound kids (and their parents) are likely figuring out what they need to pack for school — and that includes mobile phone plans. For those who want their mobile independence, T-Mobile has launched Student Perks discounts that can cost as little as $30 a month (for the Essentials Saver plan with AutoPay enabled). A limit of two students can be on the account.

And for those living off-campus in need of fast internet for all-night writing sessions, T-Mobile is offering a Student Perks bundle of 5G Home Internet for $30 a month. The deal also includes up to $200 back in virtual prepaid card credit when signing up for the service.

Tech.title: Malwarebytes Offers US College Students 2 Years of Free Antivirus Protection
Tech.content:
Malwarebytes, one of CNET.com’s Best Antivirus Overall Editors’ Choice award picks, is offering students at US colleges and universities two free years of its Malwarebytes Premium Security software suite through its Student Protection Program. The offer includes coverage for up to three devices.

Malwarebytes built its reputation on malware removal before expanding into a full antivirus suite with phishing and scam protection, ransomware defense and ad blocking. In our 2026 review, CNET’s testing team praised Malwarebytes as “an excellent choice for anyone who wants reliable security software for three or fewer devices,” awarding it our coveted Editors’ Choice badge and tying it with Bitdefender for the Best Antivirus Overall.

A representative for Malwarebytes didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Student Protection Program is open to students 18 or older enrolled at colleges and universities in the US who can produce a .edu or .college email address. The fine print on Malwarebytes’ site says it’s limiting the availability to the US, but may eventually expand the program globally. Students can check whether their school is eligible by entering their email address at the Malwarebytes website. There’s an option to request early access for schools not on the list or to fall back on a 50% student discount instead.

For students who qualify, the program unlocks the full Premium Security Standard tier. That includes real-time malware and ransomware protection, phishing and scam detection, and ad and tracker blocking. While Malwarebytes recommends a setup of one laptop, one phone and one tablet, students can use the three device slots however they choose. Once the two-year period ends, students can either keep using a limited free version without features such as real-time protection, automatic updates, and scheduled scans, or switch to a Premium subscription, which currently costs $60 per year.

The timing lines up nicely with the back-to-school season. Move-in time at a new institution means connecting unfamiliar devices to unfamiliar networks, downloading course software from links sent via email, and juggling phishing attempts disguised as financial aid notices or campus IT alerts. It can be a bit of an information security minefield, tough to add to the already overwhelming experience of school. Free access to trusted security software can at least take one thing off a student’s already crowded plate.

Tech.title: Planets, Meteors and a Solar Eclipse: August Is Going to Be a Big Month for Skygazing
Tech.content:
If you’ve been staying inside all summer due to heat waves and poor air quality from the wildfires, August is shaping up to be a good month to get out of the house and look up at the sky. Among the various cool events happening is a planet parade with six planets visible at once.

The show starts the evening of Aug. 12 and continues until around Aug. 17 or 18, depending on your location. This planet parade includes Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, Uranus, Saturn and Neptune, and like most prior parades, the planets line up on a nice curve, so it should be a little easier to see all of them. The parade is visible across the US and Canada.

You need to wake up early for this one, as the best time to see the parade is just before sunrise. This is due to Jupiter and Mercury not popping up above the eastern horizon until about 15 to 20 minutes before the sun. The good news is that Mercury and Jupiter are right next to each other and typically quite visible. A pair of binoculars should help immensely, but make sure to be careful since the sun will follow Mercury and Jupiter over the horizon in pretty short order.

The rest of the planets are much higher in the sky and present less of a visual risk. Mars is higher in the eastern sky and is visible without the need for visual aids. Uranus will be higher in the eastern sky, trending south. Following that curve, you can see Saturn in the southern sky as a yellowish dot. Neptune is nearby at the end of the line. Uranus and Neptune require a telescope or high-powered binoculars to view, and if you want a superior view of Saturn, that amplification will help too.

You have about a week if you want to do this. Before Aug. 12, Jupiter trends too close to the sun to be safely visible, and after around Aug. 17-18, Mercury ends up too close to the sun to be viewed safely. Before and after that date, you can still see a five-planet parade for quite some time.

Venus is also technically visible at night. It sets along the western horizon just after sunset, so it’s not visible at the same time as Mercury and Jupiter. However, if you don’t mind pulling an all-nighter, you can see all seven planets in the sky on the same night.

Do I need any amplification devices for this?

The inclusion of Neptune and Uranus means that you will need some sort of amplification device to see all the planets. Binoculars work, as both Uranus and Neptune can be seen (albeit faintly) with a good pair, and they’ll also help you see Mercury before sunrise.

A telescope is a much better tool since you can more easily see the rings of Saturn along with the other planets. We don’t recommend using a telescope to find Mercury, since you may accidentally catch the sun, which is not a good idea.

The Perseids meteor shower and the planet parade are visible at exactly the same time. Stellarium

Part of a triple feature coming on Aug. 12

If you’re looking for one single day to go out and view the sky for the rest of the year, Aug. 12 makes a compelling case. The planet parade ramps up then, and continues for the next week. It is always fun to see a bunch of planets from the solar system in a single night, but in terms of thrill, it’s arguably the least interesting thing happening on Aug. 12.

The Perseids meteor shower is set to peak on the evening of Aug. 12, which means those who go out to see all the planets can virtually guarantee some meteor sightings as well, since Perseids is one of the most active meteor showers of the year. In a fortuitous turn of events, the Perseus constellation, the point from which the Perseid meteors appear to originate, is right next to Mars and Uranus. That means you can scout out the parade and see meteors at the same time since they’re in the same part of the sky. The timing and placement don’t get much better than that.

If that isn’t cool enough, nature has one more thing to toss into the equation: Aug. 12 is also the date of the next solar eclipse. North America is largely sitting this one out, but if you draw a line from Washington state to North Carolina, all the states north of that line will get at least a partial solar eclipse with about 20% coverage. Since the sun isn’t completely covered, proper safety measures for solar eclipse viewing are highly advisable to avoid eye injuries.

Three prominent celestial events happening in one 24-hour span are pretty rare, so if you’re up for it, it’s a great day to look up.

Tech.title: Equifax Customers Have a Month to Claim a Piece of $2.2M Class Action Settlement
Tech.content:
If you used Equifax’s consumer credit reports service in 2022, you may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit, Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC, alleged that Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports, and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.
